summary:
The book says nothing about Joel beyond "Joel son of Pethuel" (1:1). It names no king and no datable event; proposed dates range from the ninth century BC to the fourth. The occasion is a locust plague: "What the devouring locust has left, the swarming locust has eaten" (1:4) — the full verse uses four different Hebrew words for locust. The temple's grain and drink offerings fail (1:9), and Joel reads the plague as a foretaste of "the Day of the LORD" (1:15), the prophets' term for God intervening to judge and to save.

Chapter 2 pictures the invader as an army: "they scale the walls like men of war" (2:7). Whether this is the swarm in battle imagery, a human invasion it foreshadows, or the final Day itself is debated; Joel calls it a "northern army" (2:20). At the center stands the appeal: "return to Me with all your heart" (2:12); "So rend your hearts and not your garments" (2:13) — to rend is to tear, and torn clothing was the customary sign of grief. The basis is God's character declared at Sinai: "For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion" (2:13; Exodus 34:6). God answers: "I will repay you for the years eaten by locusts" (2:25).

Then the horizon widens: "And afterward, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions" (2:28) — even on servants, male and female (2:29). Peter announces its fulfillment at Pentecost, the festival seven weeks after Passover (Acts 2:16–21); the promise "everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved" (2:32) reappears in Romans 10:13. Chapter 3 summons the nations to judgment in "the Valley of Jehoshaphat" (3:2) — Jehoshaphat means "the LORD judges" — and mirrors the swords-into-plowshares image of Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3: "Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruning hooks into spears" (3:10). The book closes with mountains dripping with sweet wine, a spring flowing from the temple, and the last line: "For the LORD dwells in Zion" (3:21) — Zion, the temple hill of Jerusalem.
